title: Pardons David Hossein Safavian
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to David Hossein Safavian as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On February 18, 2020, President Donald Trump pardoned David Hossein Safavian. The Justice Department lists a District of Columbia conviction for obstruction and three false-statement counts, with a sentence of 72 months in prison and two years of supervised release. The public clemency entry does not give the reason for the pardon.
description_long: David Hossein Safavian received a presidential pardon from Donald Trump on February 18, 2020. His federal case was in the District of Columbia and resulted in convictions for obstruction and three false-statement counts. The Justice Department records a sentence of 72 months in prison and two years of supervised release, imposed after the October 2006 case. The pardon came more than thirteen years after that case date. The public clemency record lists the offense and punishment but does not explain the underlying conduct, any clemency petition, or the administration’s reason for granting relief. Safavian’s pardon changed the federal clemency status associated with those offenses; the listing does not indicate that it erased the conviction or establish a claim of innocence. The event is therefore a specific act of executive clemency for a former federal official convicted of obstruction and false statements. Its rationale, any advocacy, and any personal or political benefit are not documented in the clemency entry. Those details should be established independently before interpreting the grant as favoritism or an exchange.

title: Pardons Peter E. Clay
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Peter E. Clay as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 13, 2021, President Donald Trump pardoned Peter E. Clay, whose Middle District of Florida case involved two counts of making false statements. The Justice Department lists a sentence of 60 months' imprisonment, 200 hours of community service, and a $10,000 fine. The clemency record gives no reason for the grant.
description_long: Peter E. Clay received a presidential pardon from Donald Trump on January 13, 2021. His Middle District of Florida case involved two convictions for making false statements. The Department of Justice lists a sentence of 60 months’ imprisonment conditioned on 200 hours of community service, plus a $10,000 fine; the case date shown is May 19, 2014. The entry does not describe the statements or identify what information was false. It also does not explain why the administration selected Clay for clemency or identify any petition or advocate. The sentence’s combination of prison time, community service, and a fine is the case-specific context the clemency list makes public. A pardon is not a reversal of the historical conviction; the record continues to identify the charges and sentence even though the president granted clemency. Nothing in the published listing establishes a personal relationship with Trump, political favoritism, or an exchange. The pardon and its recipient are documented, but the reason for the grant is not provided.

title: Pardons Dustin Laurent Heard
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Dustin Laurent Heard as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On December 22, 2020, President Donald Trump pardoned Dustin Laurent Heard, whose District of Columbia case involved six voluntary-manslaughter counts, 11 attempted-manslaughter counts, and firearm offenses. The Justice Department lists a 151-month prison sentence and 36 months of supervised release. Its entry does not describe the incident or the reason for the pardon.
description_long: On December 22, 2020, Donald Trump pardoned Dustin Laurent Heard, whose federal case involved six counts of voluntary manslaughter, eleven attempted-manslaughter counts, and firearm offenses. The Justice Department lists a 151-month prison sentence and 36 months of supervised release, with the sentence amended in September 2019. These counts describe a case involving multiple deaths and attempted killings, together with firearms used in connection with crimes of violence. The clemency entry does not describe the underlying incident, evidence, or trial proceedings, so those circumstances cannot be inferred from the charge list alone. It also provides no reason for the pardon or information about who advocated for it. The record documents the offenses and sentence covered by the grant, but not the administration’s basis for selecting Heard. The pardon should therefore be described as a federal clemency action following a serious criminal judgment without claiming a motive, personal connection, or improper exchange that the record does not establish.

title: Pardons Russell Paul Plaisance
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Russell Paul Plaisance as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On December 23, 2020, President Donald Trump pardoned Russell Paul Plaisance, whose Western District of Louisiana case involved conspiring to import cocaine into the United States. The Justice Department lists a three-year prison term that was suspended, followed by probation and special parole. The clemency list does not state a reason for the pardon.
description_long: The Justice Department's clemency list records a pardon for Russell Paul Plaisance on December 23, 2020. His case in the Western District of Louisiana involved a conspiracy to unlawfully import cocaine into the United States. The sentence shown was a three-year prison term that had been suspended, three years of probation, and three years of special parole running concurrently. The conviction date listed is November 18, 1987, more than three decades before the pardon. The suspended term means the entry does not say that Plaisance served three years in prison; it describes the sentence imposed and the supervision that followed. The DOJ list gives no account of the conspiracy's circumstances, any clemency petition, or the administration's rationale. It supports reporting the offense, sentence, and pardon date, but not an explanation for why Trump granted relief. The existence of a pardon by itself does not establish political favoritism or an exchange, and no such motive is documented here.

The Justice Department lists 30 days' imprisonment, 24 months of supervised release, and a $4,000 fine. The clemency entry does not give a reason for the pardon.
description_long: Todd A. Boulanger was pardoned by President Donald Trump on January 19, 2021. The Justice Department lists his case in the District of Columbia as a conspiracy to commit honest-services wire fraud. His sentence was 30 days in prison, 24 months of supervised release, and a $4,000 fine; the conviction date recorded is October 14, 2011. The clemency action followed nearly a decade after that case. The public entry does not describe the underlying scheme, the people or institutions affected, or any request for executive relief. It also does not explain why Boulanger received a pardon on the final day of Trump's presidency. The case listing provides enough information to distinguish the grant from a commutation and identify the federal offense and punishment at issue. It does not show that the pardon reversed the conviction, establish innocence, or prove an improper relationship or exchange. The rationale for the grant remains undocumented in the material supplied.

title: DHS proposes ending the 60-day grace period after temporary workers lose jobs
description_short: DHS proposes ending the 60-day grace period after temporary workers lose jobs
description_medium: The administration proposed removing the 60-day period during which certain temporary visa holders, including H-1B workers, can seek a new sponsor after losing their jobs. The proposal would require departure when employment ended and was open for public comment for two months. It was a proposed rule, not a change that had already taken effect.
description_long: The Trump administration proposed ending the 60-day grace period that lets certain temporary visa holders look for a new sponsor after losing their jobs. The affected categories included H-1B workers. Reuters reported the proposal on September 10, 2026, describing a rule that would require departure when employment ended. The administration opened a two-month public-comment period, leaving the proposal subject to review before any final rule. If adopted, it would shorten the time workers could use to find a new employer willing and able to sponsor them, potentially affecting workers changing jobs and employers seeking to hire people already in the United States. The proposal did not itself end the existing grace period or require immediate departures. Its status as a proposal is essential to understanding the event: the practical consequences depended on whether DHS finalized the rule and what terms it adopted after receiving comments. The available account documents the proposed change and comment period, but gives no final rule or later implementation outcome. No estimates of how many workers would be affected are included.
